beats.lead: The bug lived in exactly five cells of a chip built from thousands of them.
beats.text: The Pentium's division circuit used a lookup table with 2,048 cells; 1,066 were meant to hold real values, and five that should have held +2 held 0 instead.
beats.note: A fabrication error, not a design mistake: the array was correct on paper.

beats.name: Thomas Nicely
beats.role: maths professor at Lynchburg College, found it while counting twin primes

beats.text: Nicely noticed the inconsistency on 13 June 1994, spent four months ruling out his own code and hardware, then reported it to Intel on 24 October.
beats.note: Byte magazine later estimated only 1 in 9 billion random divisions would ever hit the bad cells.

beats.text: Intel's first response was to replace chips only for customers who could prove they were affected.
beats.note: It reversed course on 20 December 1994, after IBM halted shipments of Pentium-based PCs.

beats.context: dollars Intel charged against earnings on 17 January 1995 to cover the recall, computing's first full chip recall.

beats.line: Five wrong cells led to a $475 million recall.
